utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties wanted to raise preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the Prosecution it was simply to inquire about the RM070 application again. We would like to send a letter that we had brought to the Court's attention by the end of the week if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can refresh the Chamber's recollection but we would have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honours. Good morning, and once again a request from the Defence team. We are expecting the Trial Chamber's decision regarding the four-day week work during the coming weeks. The reason this is cropping up again is that yesterday after the session, we were in the Detention Unit. We spoke with our client. He did not feel very well, so our request would be along those lines. It's very hard for us, actually, to communicate with him, so we would like to see when the decision could be forthcoming. In our contacts we were told that the information was provided to the Trial Chamber. We don't know whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can inform you that the Chamber is making progress in preparing the decision, without saying much more. That means that it's likely that it will be -- it will be delivered sometime next week, but I'm not going to give any promises because finally all of the Chamber has to agree on the exact wording of the decision, and sometimes that goes quickly and sometimes that takes a bit more time. But we're working hard on it, you can be assured of that. If there's nothing else, is the Prosecution ready to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom tell. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to announce a housekeeping session. The Chamber announces its intention to hold a housekeeping session on or near the last sitting day of the trial, before the start of the summer recess, with the goal of disposing of as many MFIs -- MFI exhibits as possible. The Chamber, therefore, requests that the Registry provide the parties with an updated list of MFI exhibits by Wednesday, the 10th of July. The Chamber will, before that date, provide the parties with a list of the MFI exhibits for which it is awaiting further submissions so that these can be dealt with at the housekeeping session. This is the end of this announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gavric, I take it. Mr. Gavric before you give evidence the Rules require you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Gavric, you'll first be examined by Ms. Harbour. You'll find Ms. Harbour to your right. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Harbour, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My name is Mico Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying at this Tribunal in the Popovic trial on the 1st and 2nd of October, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you listen to a recording of that testimony prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As I've explained to you, we're only going to tender the portion of your prior testimony relating to the terrain sweep on the 17th of July, 1995. The Trial Chamber has that before them, and you identified several things in that testimony that should be clarified, so I'm going to go through that with you now. First, in your Popovic testimony, you talked about three children who were among the prisoners captured on 17 July 1995. And for the record, the pages where you discuss three children are transcript page 26493, 26494, 26596 and 26625, and 26626. Now, Mr. Gavric, without providing any additional details at this stage, could you please tell the Chamber now how many children you recall from that group of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I have to apologise to the Trial Chamber. At the time I said that it was three, but probably in the euphoria I made a mistake. It was four children, and now I know their names also.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. First, we'll finish with the corrections to your prior testimony. In your Popovic testimony, you testified at page 26514 that on the 17th of July you received oral orders from the Bratunac Brigade commander at noon. What time was it that you actually received these orders?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I received the orders at 10.00, and then at 10.30 up to 11.00 I went to the terrain where I was supposed to go. This was Sandici hill. And then at 11.30, between 11.00 and 12.00, I met the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, my brigade, at a slope of the Sandici hill because that was when he set off to go into the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. For now we are just correcting your prior testimony, so I would ask that we keep this as short as possible. At page 26488 of your Popovic testimony, you testified that you set off to perform the sweep at 12.00 or 12.30, and I see that you have just corrected that in your prior answer to say that you set off at 10.30 up to 11.00. And one final correction that I would ask you to make, actually two more corrections. In the Popovic testimony at transcript page 26513 you testified that you arrived at Sandici at 12.15, and I would like to ask you what actually happened at 12.15 at Sandici hill?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At 12.15, we set off to execute the assignment, and at 12.00 we were at Sandici hill -- or, rather, we joined up there with the commander of the Bratunac Battalion, Dragan Zekic, and the commander of the special detachment of the police, Dusko Jevic. That was my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And one final correction to your prior testimony is at transcript page 26490, which refers to units of the "military brigade" that participated in the sweep. Now, you've told me that this is a translation error, and what should that actually say?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It should state the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, with these corrections, if you were asked the same questioned today that you were asked during the Popovic proceedings would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Ninety-nine per cent the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You say 99 per cent. Did you have additional corrections, specific corrections that you wanted to make to your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I mean. If you were to put the questions to me, I don't know if the word order would be exactly the same. That's the kind of thing I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: But they would be the same -- your answers would be the same in substance, would they not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And would your answers be truthful and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as they have been up to now, they would continue to be so; correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the excerpts of this witness's prior testimony into evidence. The 65 ter numbers are 28913 and 28914.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. No objections, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28913 receives number P1691. And document 28914 receives number P1692, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1691 and P1692 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And P1692, can I ask that that be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1692 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would also like to tender into evidence five associated exhibits that are discussed in this tendered testimony. Four of them can be public, so I will list those first: 65 ter 4233, 19222, 4236, and 4237. And the last exhibit which I would tender should be under seal, and that's 65 ter 6144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign numbers one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4233 receives number P1693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1693 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19222 receives number P1694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1694 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4236 receives number P1695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1695 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4237 receives number P1696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1696 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 6144 receives number P1697 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1697 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would now like to lead a public summary of the witness's 92 ter evidence for the record, and I've explained the purpose of this summary to Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: On Monday, 17 July 1995, at around 10.00 a.m. Mico Gavric met at the Bratunac Brigade command with his commander, Colonel Blagojevic. Colonel Blagojevic told Gavric that he was going to Zepa. He ordered Gavric to take part in a sweep of the terrain from Sandici to Konjevic Polje. The purpose of the sweep operation was to make sure that no members of Muslim forces remained in the area. Blagojevic ordered Gavric to co-ordinate several units in the sweep including the Bratunac Brigade 3rd Battalion under Dragan Zekic and the special MUP units under Dusko Jevic. The units split up to cover the entire terrain. On the afternoon of the 17th of July, one of the units from the 3rd Battalion captured approximately 38 Muslims who surrendered in Burnice. They were arrested and brought to Pervani. There, Gavric instructed the soldiers to remove the children from the captured group. One of the soldiers was threatening one of the minors but Gavric ordered him not to hurt the children. Gavric instructed the VRS soldiers to bind the prisoners' hands. Gavric called the Bratunac Brigade command to report about the captured prisoners and ask what should be done with them. Colonel Blagojevic was not at the command because he had already left for operations in Zepa. Momir Nikolic told Gavric that Dusko Jevic should take the prisoners to a warehouse in Konjevic Polje. Gavric handed the adults over to Jevic's unit. He had the children taken to the Bratunac Brigade where he took them to the military police headquarters. Gavric arranged for a media team to film them the next morning. On 18 July 1995, the children were exchanged for several Serb police officers. Later that same day, Gavric went to Konjevic Polje. He recognised some of the prisoners he had picked up the day before. They were outside the warehouse in Konjevic Polje picking up trash. Gavric did not know what happened to the prisoners after he left Konjevic Polje. This concludes the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any additional questions, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, in 1995, what was your position in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: From the 14th of November, 1992, when the Bratunac Brigade was formed, I was assigned as the chief of artillery of the Bratunac Brigade at which duty I remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I had the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, let's turn now to the 17th of July, 1995. Bearing in mind that the Chamber has your prior testimony on this event in hand, please be careful to keep your answers strictly to what I'm asking you. In Popovic you testified at T26488 and T26513 that you were briefed by Commander Blagojevic regarding your tasks for the terrain sweep on 17th July, and you've clarified this morning that this briefing took place at 10.00 a.m. Without providing additional details, could you please tell the Chamber where did you meet Blagojevic for this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At the Bratunac Brigade command, in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've clarified for the Court this morning that you set off for the sweep at around 10.30 to 11.00 a.m. When did you next see Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that I saw Colonel Blagojevic between 11.00 and 12.00 -- or actually, around 11.30, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At a pass of Sandici hill where I was supposed to join up with the two units.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Why was Colonel Blagojevic at Sandici hill?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic was not at Sandici hill. He was just passing, because the road along which he was moving on the way to his assignment is the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Han Pijesak-Zepa road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And where was he heading?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He was going to Zepa with the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P1581 on the monitors, and this should not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Gavric, this is an intercept dated 17 July 1995 at 12.20. Let me draw your attention to about a third of the way down the page where M says that 400 set off at 1130 hours. M goes on to say there are seven buses. Then toward the bottom of the page he says, "Blagojevic set off at the head." Now, based on your interactions with Blagojevic on that date, do you know what this intercepted conversation is about?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that this has to do with the movement of the Bratunac Brigade. It's moving to its assignment. I don't know how many buses there were, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, in the Popovic case you testified at transcript page 26598 that during the course of the sweep operation prisoners were captured in the Burnice area and then arrested and brought to the area of Pervani. Could you please describe this place near Pervani where the prisoners were brought?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When a certain number of people were captured in the Burnice village area, those same people were brought to the Pervani area. The Pervani area where the people were brought is at the end of the Lolici village and at the beginning of the Pervani village. It's on the left side of the road as you go from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje; that's one thing. The other thing is that the asphalt road in that sector where the people were captured, there is a concrete water fountain. So that would be one feature which was some 400 metres east from the Pervani mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Were the prisoners armed when they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: All the prisoners who surrendered wore civilian clothes, whereas the troops in the field had brought with them a lot of infantry weapons that the soldiers and other armed people had carried with them in their attempt to break out towards Tuzla. They had probably discarded the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: But the prisoners who surrendered, you said they wore civilian clothes. Could you also confirm that they were not armed?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. They were brought to us unarmed, but whether they were unarmed while moving, I cannot possibly know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, in Popovic, at transcript page 26493, you testified that the children were brought back to the Bratunac Brigade on the evening of the 17th of July. What time did you arrive back at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time now, but I believe it was around 7.30 p.m., not later than 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And at T26597 in Popovic you testified that the children were filmed by a TV crew. Who arranged for the children to be filmed?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I returned from the field, I went to see the duty operations officer, and that was Major Filipovic. So when I returned and reported from my field mission, I also mentioned there were four children there. They should be given media coverage, TV crews should be brought, and it was the job of the assistant commander for morale. Ratko was his first name. I don't remember his last name. He was a major, and he was assistant commander for morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: When did the filming take place?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 4239 on the monitors. We're bringing up a Bratunac 1st Light Infantry Brigade command document which is dated 17 July 1995 and written to the Drina Corps command. This document reads, and I quote: "Among the Muslim prisoners, there are four underaged children, aged between 8 and 14, who are being held in military custody in Bratunac." And then the last sentence of the document reads: "We propose that this testimony be recorded by cameras of your press centre." And at the bottom we see that it was delivered on 18 July 1995 at 12.40 in the morning. Is this document related to the events that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: From what I know, people from the press centre were supposed to come in the morning and do the filming, but I was not at the brigade command, so I don't know if they had stuck to that arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you provide the information that's contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I only provided information that they passed on to the press centre to the effect that the children were aged 8 to 14, and all the rest was up to the assistant commander for morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And we can see that the document -- at the bottom of the document is written "Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic." Was he present at the brigade command when you brought the children back?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There was no one there at the time, only Major Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I please tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] document 04239 receives number P --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 04239 receives number P1698, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1698 is admitted into evidence. Have you done with the filming, Ms. Harbour, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have one or two additional questions. In your previous testimony, you said: "We filmed the children so that there would be no news circulating the globe that children were being caught and shot." What raised your concern about possibly such news circulating the globe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every war brings with it a lot of dirty things, and so did our war. Propaganda is at the forefront of the special war. My main aim was, first and foremost, to protect these children, because if they are given media coverage and filmed, then nobody would dare even think about doing something ugly to them. Second, apart from taking care of their lives, I also took care of the morale of my brigade and my own conscience, and I thought my army would not be seen as killing young or the infirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there at that moment any media reports about prisoners or whether children are not being ill-treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war I followed electronic media, and they were all engaged in propaganda rather than concerned with the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The days before you filmed those kids, was there any specific media attention you noticed about the fate and the treatment of persons which had left Srebrenica after it fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know so much about that, but now I know that B92 was present at many locations where certain actions took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you knew at the time. So you're saying you were following the electronic media, but there was no specific attention to the Srebrenica Muslims which had left, that there was no media attention to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time, there was no talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what then suddenly caused you to take these measures, whereas -- what then triggered that exactly, just a general concern about possible media attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said a moment ago once you have a child, you start giving them an upbringing. My parents had six children, and they always told us, Do no evil so that no one would do evil to you. That's one. Two, at school, at the school for reserve officers and throughout life, I learned that lesson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I asked whether there was any specific media attention in that moment that would have triggered it where you said it was just a general awareness of the possibility of propaganda and that at that point in time, although following the electronic media, you said there was no specific attention for the fate of Muslims which had left Srebrenica. Is that how -- that's how I understood your answer. Now, is that -- can you confirm that I have understood your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you understood that correctly, but regarding media coverage for the children, that could not happen until somebody calls up the media and tells them about that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my next question would be you said you also -- media coverage would protect the children, because no one would dare to touch them if they had been filmed. Now, these children were in the custody of your own army or your own units. Was there any specific reason why you had to protect them under those circumstances, because usually filming is used as protection by those who have to fear something from the situation in which the filmed persons find themselves, and they were in your own hands. So what were they to be protected for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to take some time to answer this. First and foremost, my job as the commanding officer sent by the Bratunac Brigade was not allow in the field, in case somebody's captured, any trouble or any killing. And I was perfectly aware that anyone who surrenders and gets killed while I was in command of that unit I would be held to account; that's one. Two, regarding the children, I had a clash - as Miss or Madam Prosecutor said a while ago - I had a clash with one of the soldiers who was a volunteer and expressed his wishes in that regard which I did not acknowledge. I put a stop to it and did not allow him to do what he wanted. Also, I couldn't be with the children all the time, and by ensuring that media coverage I ensured that they would be safe, even in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there at any moment anyone including yourself who sought to film any adult prisoners in order to protect them to what might happen to them? Exposing them to the media would have protected them as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer. When these people were captured, they were all in civilian clothes. As far as I know, and I was a uniformed military man, these people did not belong to me as a military unit to do anything about them. I had turned them over to the civilian police which was in charge of civilians. Second, the people who were taken to Konjevic Polje escorted by Dusko Jevic, that seemed logical to me that they would be taken to Konjevic Polje instead of Bratunac, because from Konjevic Polje I thought they would be taken to the collection centre in Batkovici near Bijeljina. That's what I knew about that centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not really an answer to my question, but, Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, you testified at transcript page 26611 in the Popovic case that the children were exchanged on the 18th of July, 1995. Can you tell me how this exchange or -- was arranged and who was involved?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 18th, I spoke to Ljubisa Borovcanin because Ljubisa Borovcanin had found out about those children and asked me if he could get them to carry out an exchange. Nine members of the Special Police in Doboj were detained in the area of Zvornik. I said it was possible and that we intended to take the children to the separation line and let them go to the territory of the federation, behind the separation line. I told him, Ljubisa, there is no problem, but please make sure that these children get to the place that is arranged. He said, Don't worry. In the meantime, an open vehicle, PUH, with only a driver in it, and he took those children. So on the 18th the children were turned over to this man sent by Ljubisa Borovcanin, and I believe on the same day or the 19th they were exchanged. In my mind, it stayed as the 18th, because that's when they left the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Can you describe this open vehicle which you called "PUH"?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It's a vehicle which has a metal cab at the front and one part of the roof. In the back the rest of the vehicle is covered by a tarpaulin which is removed in summertime. I believe the vehicle had belonged to the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, you testified in Popovic at transcript page 26493 and 26595 that Dusko Jevic took the adult prisoners to Konjevic Polje, that the next day you went through Konjevic Polje and that in front of a warehouse in Konjevic Polje you saw a group of people picking up paper and litter who you recognised as the prisoners from the previous day. How did you know that they were the same prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, I was going to Sokolac where I had personal business, and passing through Konjevic Polje I saw a group of people around that depot. Out of sheer curiosity I stopped to see if those were the same people, and when I tried to approach, one of those policemen stopped me, but he let me go relatively quickly. I suppose that his commander was close by, that he recognised me and let me come in. They were collecting litter, paper mostly, around the depot. So I recognised 95 per cent of that group among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P1132 and e-court page 50 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gavric, while this is coming up, could you tell me were they still prisoners or were these people who were picking up trash freely walking around in front of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: They were certainly prisoners. But because their hands were untied after we had turned them over to Dusko Jevic, they couldn't work with their hands tied behind their backs, so their hands were untied and they were collecting paper and other litter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And you mentioned that one of -- you said, "One of those policemen stopped me." Who was it that was guarding the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The warehouse was guarded by the same unit that had participated in the sweep with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, on the screen you can see a photograph of a landscape and some buildings and a road, and you can see that a blue arrow is pointing to a building that is circled. Do you recognise where this is and what that building is?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That is the building where those people were standing when I came on the intersection Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik-Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Is this the warehouse that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This used to be a co-operative earlier, and then in the 1990s, since I come from that area, it was a shop, and today there is a large petrol station in that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, would this be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Ms. Harbour. We take a break of 20 minutes. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. One second. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that there is another preliminary which the Prosecution would like to raise. Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It occurred to us during Mr. Gavric's testimony that he should receive a Rule 90(E) caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give him one with retroactive effect. No, no, no. That was -- we'll ask him whether there have been any moments that he would have hesitated to answer the questions. The witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Gavric, I would like to briefly deal with the following matter: You appear here as a witness. Now, if you would object to making or to answering any of the -- right channel. I see Mr. Mladic is nodding that it's okay by now. It's okay now? Yes. Mr. Gavric, a witness who when he answers a question which -- truthfully and if that answer might tend to incriminate that witness may object to answer that question. We then, however, we could compel the witness, so we could compel you to answer such a question, and then that could not be -- the answer could not be used against yourself. Now, perhaps we should have better done this at the beginning of your testimony, but was there at any moment any hesitation on your part to answer a question because you feared you might incriminate yourself? You're nodding yes. Does it mean that you did not hesitate at any moment to answer a question out of fear to incriminate yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I could not have brought myself into an incriminating position no matter what I said, because in this gesture during my command over certain assignments I adheredly strict -- I strictly adhered to the rules of service and to the orders of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, orders by the superior command do not under all circumstances relieve you from your personal responsibility, but I do understand that the subject matter did not give you any reason to think that by truthfully answering the questions that you could incriminate yourself. Nevertheless, I have drawn your attention to this Rule, and if you would object to making in the follow-up of -- in the following parts of your testimony if you would like to make an objection to make any statements, you're free to address the Chamber. Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to Exhibit P1132 and page 50 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gavric, while this is coming up, after you saw Colonel Blagojevic on Sandici hill, when did he return from the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the commander of the brigade until the 29th of July. We saw each other at a funeral of a soldier of mine who was killed. So we were together at this funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And is it your understanding that around the 29th of July was when he returned from the Zepa operation to the Bratunac Brigade area of operations?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That period from the 17th until the 29th I spent on different assignments, so I didn't have the opportunity to meet with him. I'm just saying when it was that I met with him. I went to Zeravica near Han Pijesak where we were holding a position, and he also toured the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Regardless of when you were able to meet with him, do you know when he returned from the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I really don't know the exact day. I just said when it was that I saw him for the first time after the 17th and that was the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Colonel Blagojevic toured the units near Han Pijesak. When was this?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that there was an error in the interpretation. I think that I went to go and tour one of the units near Han Pijesak at Zeravica. So that was between the 17th and the 29th of July. So I don't know exactly when he came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to draw your attention now to this photograph on the monitor. Could you tell me what is the name of that road that we see?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This road that you can see is the Zvornik-Sarajevo road. This is what you can see on the picture. The second part of the road from Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac is barely visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. And is this sometimes known as the Milici-Drinjaca road?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It depends on where you live. That's how you call it. We're talking about -- when we describe it, we use the bigger settlements that it passes through. So that's what we use.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, do you know what happened to the prisoners after you last saw them picking up trash in front of this warehouse in Konjevic Polje on 18 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Officially it's correct. I don't know. It is only in 2000 when I was here to testify, Mr. Karnavas said to me, we were talking about all of this, and he told me then that allegedly those people were dug up in the Cerska area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And who is Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Not Karnavas, I'm sorry, but Bourgon. He was the Defence attorney of the general in the proceedings. So it wasn't Karnavas but Bourgon who said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 23277 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The document that's coming up is a Zvornik CJB dispatch, and it's dated 18 July 1995. And I'd like to draw your attention to item 1 which states that the RS MUP units and the Special Police Unit combed on the right of the Milici-Drinjaca road including features behind Cerska and Udrc in order to "liquidate the remnants of infiltrated groups from Srebrenica. The action was completed very successfully." Were the prisoners that you saw at Konjevic Polje among those remnants who were liquidated?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: They could not have been among those groups that remained behind. The groups that were left behind would be covered in the terrain sweep which we carried out on the 17th. If you found any troops in that area, then that would be the remainder. These are no longer the remainder. These were people who were captured, and I said what my information was about what would happen, but they were not groups that had infiltrated the area or troops that were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And your information about what would happen, does that refer to the fact that they were dug up in the Cerska grave?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not logical to me. If this did happen, for me it would have been logical. My information as to what would have happened and that is that those people would go to Bijeljina, to Batkovic. They would be accommodated there at the reception centre and then exchanged for the remaining Serbs from the Tuzla basin. That was my information. This was the talk about that in the command. About this other part, there was never any talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, could we stay out of what is logic and what is not and whether the witness, who may have no knowledge about exactly what is written in this document, whether the witness thinks or thinks not that the ones should be part of those without proper factual foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to tender this document and move on from it. The reason I showed it to this witness is because he has testified about a sweep operation that he took part in to the right of the Milici-Drinjaca road with a Special Police Unit just as is discussed in this document, but I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that he has done that, and then of course the Chamber will evaluate, but whether this document now includes because they were captured yes or no whether it refers to those, the witness apparently has no factual knowledge about that. But he told us about his own participation in an operation which in its description seems to be similar to what we find in this document. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23277 receives number P1699, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1699 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so I would like to ask one additional question. We just looked at a document, a document about the sweeping operation and the liquidation of the remains. Do you know anything about any operations which were aiming at liquidating the remains, the remains of the enemy armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know about that bit, but generally when a superior writes an order he would say liquidate, "unistiti." You can liquidate only somebody who puts up a resistance. If they don't put up a resistance then there is no logic, for me, for this to be said in the order in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, we are trying to stay out of the field of logic and, rather, talk about facts. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, permit me first to ask you this: During those days of July 1995, did you have the opportunity to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us when and where these encounters occurred?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July in the operations centre of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret did not catch the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Could you repeat the time when you, on the 12th of July, had an encounter with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 7.00 -- at 10 minutes past 7.00 in the morning on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what sort of a meeting this was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the morning on the 11th to the 12th, I slept in my family house which is close to the Bratunac Brigade command. My assignment in the morning meant that I was obliged to report to the operations room at 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I take it that you asked the witness to slow down, but since you did it without a microphone -- he may have understood it. It's not on the record. Could you please slow down your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? At 7.00 in the morning, I came to the command compound. Since at 7.00 in the morning General Mladic had already started the meeting, I wanted to enter the operations room, and then in front of it I encountered a major who had been told to leave the meeting, and I was joking with the man, and I knocked and entered the room where the meeting was being held. The General asked me why I was late. I explained why, and then I sat down at some fourth or fifth place back that was free, and I attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what the meeting was about and if General Mladic said anything when you were there.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the topics when I had already arrived -- after a short amount of time there was Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula. I don't know if he was the commander of the Visegrad brigade. I think it was his task to continue with the sweep of the terrain in the Srebrenica area, more precisely near the school of the local community of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other orders issued by General Mladic to any one of those present?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He did not issue any orders to anyone else, only to this Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you leave the meeting before it formally ended, or did you stay until the formal closing of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I stayed longer. I was there throughout the whole time, and during that time nothing further was discussed, nor were there any orders issued, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, I would like to ask you, Mr. Gavric, in the previous answer did you say, I quote "He did issue any orders," or did you say, "He did not issue any orders to anyone else," only to Furtula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I came at 10 past 7.00 and for as long as the general was in the operations room, he only ordered Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula to -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means -- your answer was: He did not issue any orders to anyone else except Furtula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please go a bit more slowly so that everything could be recorded in the transcript. According to your recollection, at what time did General Mladic leave the Bratunac Brigade and that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was at about 8.00 that he left the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to see him again at any point in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not ever meet General Mladic again since then to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just briefly like to go through something that is very important to us. At one point did you receive an order to go to Zvornik with a part of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell the Trial Chamber who you received the order from?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I got the order on the 14th to the 15th -- or on the 15th, to be more precise, at about 12.30 from the commander Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did the order say that you received in the night between the 14th and the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 14th at zero thirty hundred hours the military police came to my family house and told me to come to the brigade command. I got ready very quickly and I came to the command. At the command in the operations room I encountered Colonel Blagojevic and Major Dragan Trisic, who was the logistics assistant. When I sat down, I said, Colonel, sir, go ahead. And then he said, Listen, I received an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really should slow down, because otherwise your words will be lost. Try to keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When I arrived at the Bratunac Brigade command, to the operations room, I saw Colonel Blagojevic there and the logistics assistant commander, Major Dragan Trisic. I sat down and I asked the colonel, Tell me what you need. And he told me that he had received an order from the superior command to send one of the units to assist in Zvornik, because there was a large concentration of Muslim forces around Zvornik. And I answered that my unit was not meant for infantry fighting. There must be other units for that. He told me, You can organise your unit the fastest and go to the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, and I'll ask you to tell the Court about the structure of that unit of yours which you said was not equipped for infantry operations.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My unit had within its composition troops who were trained from officers-plotters and gunners and their assistants, the people who pass on the shells and put them into barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So what was that group?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed artillery group because in its composition it had a battery of B1 cannons, 76 millimetres; one cannon platoon, 122 millimetres/37; and a howitzer platoon, 105 millimetres, M-56.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point did you receive that order and went to meet the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people went with you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Forty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get a promise that you would be rotated soon?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 14th-15th, when did you reach the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe 1.30, perhaps 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps out of an abundance of caution I think we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just wait to see the English version as well. I should like to draw your attention to -- that would be paragraph 2, which says, among other things -- it's not very legible, so you'll have to make a bit of an effort to read the B/C/S. The last sentence of this daily report of the Bratunac Brigade, dated 15 July 1995, that a part of the forces has been sent to the area of "Zlpbr, the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade (80 soldiers)." Would this part of the regular daily report dated 15 July be consistent with your memory that at one point your group of 40 artillery men was rotated by another part of the Bratunac Brigade? Do you remember that number?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's true we were replaced. The commander sent Major Eskic and the commander of the 1st Company of the 2nd Battalion, Zoran Kovacevic, along with these 80 soldiers. Now, whether there were 80 or 60, I really don't know. I know that they did come to Zvornik, and I took one of the buses that had brought them and returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, not all of us are familiar with that area. Could you tell us first which route did you take to go from Bratunac to Zvornik on the night of the 14th July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. At the intersection we took a right turn towards Drinjaca, then we continued on towards Zvornik town, passed it, and outside of the town 1 or 2 kilometres further was some sort of factory where the command of the Zvornik Brigade was and I took the same route back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At what time on the 15th of July did you return, taking the same road?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We departed from Zvornik around 11.00, so at noon we were back in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Travelling on that road, did you notice on the way from Konjevic Polje via Kravica and up to Bratunac any military units?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the return trip I didn't see any people, but when I was departing on Sandici hill I saw people who were guarding the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were members of the Bratunac Brigade or the police forces who were present in the area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Some of them were policemen and others were members of the Bratunac unit, but I don't know when they had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you spend the rest of the day on the 15th of July and the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from Zvornik, I got a short leave from the commander, and I spent that day and a half with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you corrected your statement on one point, namely the time when on the 17th of July you received a new order from Colonel Blagojevic. First of all, I want to ask you is that true?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Now definitively, after talking to the other men who were there, I'm sure. I got to the brigade command at the same time, and at 10.00 Colonel Blagojevic issued me the order to be -- to act as co-ordinator in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in earlier statements you mentioned that it could have been around noon on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was interpretation or something else, but that was a mistake. At noon I had agreed with Dragan Zekic and Jevic to be on Sandici hill, and at 12.15 we had already started moving along the Sandici-Kamenica and Gornji Bratunci [phoen] road deploying troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you the following: You referred to having talked to the other men who were there. You said: "Now, definitively, after talking to the other men who were there, I'm sure" that "I got to the brigade command ..." now, when did you talk with them and with whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to Major Trisic, because he was in the office next to mine and for a long time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I returned from this trial, because we discussed that time, that period, and he told me, Your memory is good, because you made the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- perhaps I'm confused. I think you recently corrected the time. Ms. Harbour, I'm also looking at you. It was in -- is the correction made -- originates from when, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- he corrected his Popovic testimony. However, he has in prior testimonies testified that the time was between 10.00 and noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you speak with the person you mentioned after you had given your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to him in October 2008, after I returned, and then taking into account his recollection and my recollection I was able to determine these things. When I came here first, I had had no earlier opportunity to -- to tell the Prosecutor about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you had talked to the men who were there. Did you talk with anyone else apart from Major Trisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the CO, Major Trisic, the people within the command, because within the command we discussed these things, but we don't discuss them with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you discussed them, therefore not only with Major Trisic but with others as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, with Major Trisic because we were close, and we continued to discuss our memories of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you said you had discussed it with the men who were there, which suggests that there was more than one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be a grammatical error, let me say, and I can ascribe it to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The place where you were supposed to meet with the unit, senior officers that were to take part in the execution of the assignment was at Sandici. What I want to know now is how far is Sandici hill far from -- from the Bratunac Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It's 13 kilometres to Kravica and then another kilometre or a kilometre and a half to Sandici hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P1694 in e-court, please, 1694. Can we go through the document briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document drafted by Colonel Ignjat Milanovic on the 15th of July, 1995, and it's sent to the Drina Corps command, to the 1st mlpbr and the SB Skelani. I am now going to ask you this: Do you know who at that time, and which duties at that time were carried out by Ignjat Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Ignjat Milanovic, as far as I can remember -- actually, I don't remember at all his duties when General Krstic took over corps command. I really don't know what duty he was occupying, whether it was operations chief or Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to meet Colonel Ignjat Milanovic during those days?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ignjat Milanovic was the Chief of Staff of the Bratunac Brigade. We knew each other very well. And, as far as I can remember, from there he went to be the commander of the Milici Brigade and then he was transferred to the Drina Corps, and he was replaced by, I think, from Bratunac -- from a -- by an officer from Bratunac, Ivan Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, would you agree with me that Colonel Ignjat Milanovic at that time in July 1995 was a senior officer at the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we now look at the first paragraph of the document where he's informing the commander and the command of the Drina Corps, and among other things, he says the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, if that's proper expansion of the abbreviation, assess the situation and is about to come out on the ordered line. I'm asking you whether the brigade already on the 15th of July or earlier had already started the terrain sweeping operation.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: All I know is that as soon as the operation in Srebrenica was finished, the battalions were assigned and sent to sweep the terrain. I didn't know about this order, because it came at the time when I was resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to deal with some doubts of mine, in the military sense. If you look at the middle part of the document where it states, "I ordered the following," and then in item 4 it says that the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade shall continue to search the terrain and clear up the battleground on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Kasaba road and create a sort of reserve of the forces because they currently do not have any in order to be able to be engaged upon request. In the control and command system, can Colonel Ignjat Milanovic issue an order of this type so that it's executed by the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As soon as he receives an order from the corps, and it must have been written in an order coming from a high place, that then the commander of subordinate units, the commanders the Bratunac and Milici Brigade were subordinated. So they had to carry out this order. So he did have the right to order the commanders that their units carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then he says "proposal 1," that the commander of the commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade is authorised and appointed as commander of all forces engaged in the sweeping of the train and the clearing up, "asanacija," of the battleground east of the road and part of the Kasaba-Drinjaca road; because in the command of the Drina Corps, if that is the proper expansion of the abbreviation, "We do not have anyone we could assign to the task." And then who is being assigned as the co-ordinator of this assignment if he does have the right to command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If certain assignments are about to begin, the superior officer must appoint a lower-ranking officer who would be responsible for that in the entire area. Like I was responsible for the police unit and the military unit in the same way, according to the way I'm thinking, the colonel could have appointed Blagojevic as the commander of that complete action in that section of the sweep operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for a minute. Would it be correct that the area that was indicated here as the area to be searched was in the territory which was behind the defence zone of a number of brigades that were part of the Drina Corps, not just the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, if the Milici Brigade is included, then, yes, because the Bratunac Brigade was sweeping the Bratunac municipality topographical area, because the place where the left flank of the Bratunac and the right flank of the Milici Brigade were joined and the area where they were sweeping the train belonged to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're speaking too quickly. You said: "... because the area where the left flank of the Bratunac and the right flank of the Milici Brigade were joined and the area where they were sweeping the terrain belonged to --" and would you then please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area assigned to both of them, meaning the right flank of the Milici Brigade, left flank of the Bratunac Brigade, bordered on each other territorially, both according to the boundaries of the municipalities and according to the boundaries of the assignments that were assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if the sweeping of the terrain, and I'm asking you as a senior officer and a military person, is a legitimate activity after that kind of combat?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an obligation. In order to secure the terrain you need to sweep the terrain, just as it would happen if a terrorist group is infiltrated into a country. When the terrorist group is destroyed, then you are obliged to sweep the terrain again and sanitise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. Time for a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber was informed that there is a possibility that you would conclude your cross-examination within the next hour. Is that -- yes. That would be highly appreciated, because the Chamber needs a bit of time for some procedural matters as well. Could you give us already an assessment what time the Prosecution would need for re-examination if any?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At this stage we don't anticipate having any redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll both have time to conclude the testimony of the witness and to deal with the procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped, sir, at the point when we were talking about the area and the legitimacy of actions relating to the sweeping of the terrain. Is it correct that this area was deep inside territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska before the operation to free Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite deep inside that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in this document, I think you still have it in front of you, the term "asanacija" is mentioned. As an officer, I want to ask you if you know what that term implied as it stood in the order of Ignjat Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Looking at this order now, I'm surprised to see that it says that you could -- you should do the sanitisation of the terrain together with the sweep, because that is something that is done after the sweep operation is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you're an artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you completed the non-commissioned officers' school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When and where in?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In 1997-1998 in Zadar, and then after that I was an intern in the 3rd Guards Regiment in Pozarevac where I worked for a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at the screen in front of you where it says that in 1997-1998 you completed the school in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is a mistake. It's a typing error. It was 1978-1979 that that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what does "asanacija," the sanitisation of the terrain, mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That means that the remnants that remain, including bodies, should be collected all at a certain location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule would that be the job of soldiers or any specialised services?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, in happier times that would be the job of the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with this document by putting the question: If you personally know if there was any order or document that Vidoje Blagojevic as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was authorised and appointed as commander of all the forces that took part in the sweep operation.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that. As I said, that order didn't reach me because that was issued during the time that I was off, I was resting. So I'm not familiar with this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to this order that you received from Blagojevic on the 17th of July at approximately 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. I am asking you do you remember exactly the wording? What exactly was your task?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was ordered by the corps -- the brigade commander to go to Kravica, to Konjevic Polje, to be more precise where Dragan Zekic and Dusko Jevic were: Dragan Zekic who was heading the 3rd Battalion and Dusan Jevic who was heading the Special Police detachment. I should put them together and agree with them how to proceed with the terrain sweep from Sandici through Kamenica, Gornji Bratunac and up to Konjevic Polje along the left side of the road towards Konjevic Polje from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand and were you told directly that you had any command responsibilities over the police units in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I understood that I would be there just like a co-ordinator in that area, which is what I was, and that all of the -- each of the units were given a certain zone to sweep, specifically from the road to Kamenica entrusted to the police and from Kamenica to Gornji Bratunac, that area was assigned to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the police have its own chain and system of command and control in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had company commanders who commanded in the field, and Dusko Jevic was the representative of the special detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P15882 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I assume that you had the opportunity to see this document in earlier testimony. I'm now going to ask you to look at paragraph marked 1 which says that on the 17th of July, the commander of the Special Police Brigade, Goran Savic, orders the urgent formation of a combat group the size of a battalion in the Kravica-Konjevic Polje sector using the 5th Doboj Special Police Detachment, two companies from the seminar on Jahorina and two PJP companies with the assignment of searching the terrain in the Pobudje sector, in the course of that day, the 17th of July, so as to fully mop up the right side of the Milici-Drinjaca road before regrouping for the search of Cerska. In paragraph 2, the BG commander, if that would indicate "borbena grupa," combat group, comprising units referred to in the previous item, and then the deputy commander of the Special Police would be Dusko Jevic. Would this order correspond to what you remember about the police forces which took part in sweeping the terrain in a specific area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order refers to this assignment in the Pobudje sector, but it says here that it should be 800 or 600 people from the police to be engaged. This is incorrect data. In the field where I was, I don't think that this number of people took part in the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your best recollection, how many did participate?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, up to 200 policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what is that opinion based, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am basing my opinion on the fact that when we lined up the units at Sandici hill that's the number, and then judging by the area in which we deployed them after we issued assignments to the police when they were there, I went with Dusko Jevic and at a certain -- and the soldiers were at a certain distance apart from each other. So when you cover that area, the number that you would get according to these calculations would not be more than 200 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not that much interested in calculations or reconstructions but rather in facts, and I do understand that you saw the men lined up and you saw men at a certain distance and then you started calculating. Mr. Stojanovic, please next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you go to the next question, I just want to find out from the witness if he could please direct us to where the numbers 800 and 600 are referred to in this document. I understand that he --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer this question by the Judge. How did you get this number 800?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: According to this order if the unit from Jahorina was engaged and they were present and the other units enumerated here in this order did not take part in the sweep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the question was: How did you come up with this claim that 800 policemen were supposed to be involved?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, there are four detachments mentioned here, if I see well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go step-by-step. I believe it is written in item 1, please follow this, that the following should be engaged: The 5th Special Police detachment Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to waste your time. Obviously the witness is not able to give us where he finds the number 800 or 600 from this document and you don't have to go through all those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I would like to get a clarification from the witness. On page 49, lines 14 to 18, the witness said, "This order referred to this assignment in the Pobudje sector," but it says here that "it should be 800 or 600 people from the police to be engaged." Is that -- Mr. Gavric, is that just the consequence of your calculation, or how could you say that, that it says here it should be 800 or 600 people from the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order perhaps to cut matters short having listened to the questions, having listened to you, Witness, do I understand you well that your reference to 800 to 600 people was a calculation based on the units mentioned in the order and that then later you say, That must be wrong because what I saw on the ground, and then you started calculating again coverage, terrain, et cetera, that it should have been less? Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how you should understand my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, all -- both the initial numbers and the later numbers all based on calculations rather than on any exact knowledge of facts. It's interpretation of the document and then interpretation of what you saw on the ground. Mr. Stojanovic, you may put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just wrap this up. According to your estimate of what you saw when you lined up the participants in this operation, how many policemen and soldiers were there in total?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Around 500 policemen and soldiers in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally go in depth of the area where the units were moving?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be told not to start answering before the question is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters ask you not to start your answer until the question has been translated. The best way of doing it is look at your screen and once the text stops moving, as, for example, it did now, that you only then start giving an answer. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, did you have an organised system of communications between the commanding officers of the units that were involved in the sweep?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information as to whether during the sweep the units were coming across dead bodies in the area they were passing through?
