utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There were corpses on the line from which we started the sweep and along the whole length of the road, 50 metres wide and all along, there were corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea, taking into account the markings you made in the previous case, what is the width of the area where you conducted the sweep, and what is the length?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The width is 6 kilometres, and the depth was 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who kept you informed that they were finding bodies in this area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When assignments were given and soldiers deployed, above Kamenica was the transit area where columns of people breaking out towards Tuzla were moving. In that area, one part is wooded and the other part isn't. The wooded part of the area is cut through by a small track leading to Gornje Vratnice, which is where our people were moving through. They were coming across a lot of corpses that were hanging, people who had hanged themselves. A large number of corpses was lying on the ground, with lower parts of the bodies destroyed, probably by setting bombs underneath their own bodies. You could see that some had committed suicide, usually by a gunshot to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the sweep did you receive information from the units involved that they were coming across military equipment and weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I could see that for myself, because each of our soldiers involved in that operation had taken -- or, rather, had brought with him back one or two rifles of different makes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I seek some clarification of one of the previous answers. You said: "There were coming across a lot of people who were hanged. They were hanging. The lower parts of the bodies were destroyed, probably by bombs set below them ..." Now, how do I have to understand that? Is it that people hang themselves and then someone would put a bomb under their body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to make this clearer. I found a lot of people who had taken off their belts and hanged themselves from trees. That's one type of death. Another type of death is when people put a bomb under themselves. When I said the lower part of the body, I meant the part of the body lying on the ground. And judging by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've read all that in your previous testimony, but today you combine even the two. You say: “ They were hanging, the lower parts of the bodies were destroyed, probably by bombs set below them ..." This suggests that people hanging had even destroyed lower part of their body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know exactly how it was interpreted to you, but I can repeat. I don't mean that lower parts of the hanging bodies were destroyed. I meant to say that some people committed suicide by placing a bomb under themselves and the bomb damaged the lower part of their bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check whether there is a translation error or not or that you combined the two elements. So you did not say that those who were hanging, that they had the lower parts of their bodies destroyed. You say that's not what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll verify that. Madam Registrar, I would like to have verified as soon as possible -- let me see. It's page 54 -- no. It is page -- page 53, lines 11 to 14, even if only provisionally for the time being so that we have a provisional verification of the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During these activities related to the sweep, did you at any point have information that some other units of the Drina Corps were participating in the sweep as well?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to call up in e-court P1579.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could we please look together at paragraph 3 of this order. In the text it says that it's an order by Colonel-General Ratko Mladic dated 17 July, 1995, and it reads: "As of 17 July, the forces of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, and the 67th Military Police Battalion, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and MUP forces engaged in the wider areas of Bratunac, Milici, and Drinjaca will comb the territory in the zone of Bratunac, Drinjaca, Milici, Vecici village," et cetera. Did you at any point have information that this sweep involved also some units from the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the key issue I want to ask you about, it says here and please pay attention to the following paragraph of -- or, rather, following sentence in paragraph 3: "I hereby appoint Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, the officer for military police in the Main Staff of the VRS security administration, as the commander of all the aforementioned forces during the conduct of the aforementioned task." Do you know Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I heard that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say it was the first time, do you mean today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I mean I heard it the first time today. I never met the man, or perhaps I met the man without knowing that that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time in the course of at that day, the 17th of July, have around a commanding officer whom you didn't know and who gave you advice or instructions regarding the sweep?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time after the execution of that task on the 17th July, the 18th, or any of the other following days report to anyone else but the commanders of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No one except Filipovic, the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any time in the course of that 17th of July have any contact with the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment based at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not, because I didn't go to that area on the 17th. I passed through on the 18th, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you mentioned the place from which you started the sweep could you please explain to the Court relative to Konjevic Polje where did -- where was the boundary where that sweep area ended?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was actually 1 kilometre beyond the road, the kilometre up to the road at Djugovi -- at Djugum remained outside the sweep. Djugum is to the south of Drinjaca, 1 or 2 kilometres to the south, and that is the boundary between Bratunac and Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says the assignment is finished. You have reached the point where you were supposed to reach in the sweep of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I set off, I got the assignment of sweeping the terrain up to the part that we reached, the other part is quite forested, and according to information that I had, there were a lot of mines there, so I did not want to let my people go to that part of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your best recollection, what time of the day was it that you completed that day's work?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that it was at 1900 hours. Between 1800 and 1900 hours, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At what point in time did you get information that there were prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that this was at around 1700 hours that Dragan Zekic received information through his radio that during the sweep of the terrain a resistance was met. Dragan informed me about this, and I said then that they should not rush, not to sustain casualties, but to go slowly and to call people to surrender. Dragan conveyed this to some of his subordinate commanding officers, and then they reported back to him and he conveyed to me that shooting was over and that there was one child with a white T-shirt in his hands was walking towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there for a moment and ask: When you say that you received information that there was resistance, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what this was about? What kind of a resistance was this?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I will tell you everything. There was shooting in the direction of our units. I found this out later from these children who were there because they said that in this group there were some other people who had not surrendered, who did not wish to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did any members of the Bratunac Brigade get killed or were they wounded at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed and nobody was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any members of the police forces that took part in the action were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know we were together in that place down there when those people who were captured were brought in. Nobody said anything about it, but I would have known about it in essence because Dusko Jevic was close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who or which formation was it which you described as Cesme [phoen] on the road who brought the prisoners out?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: These were soldiers of the 3rd Battalion. I don't know which unit it was, which company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the 3rd Battalion, you mean the Bratunac Brigade Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after they were brought in as prisoners, did you count those people, and did you take down their names?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I counted the people while they were there, and then when we went and when we reached the road when they went to Konjevic Polje in a column two by two, I told Jevic, Jevic, I am taking the children with me and you take these -- these people with you. They will probably send a bus for them so that they could go to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were there in total, according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I remember 99 per cent accurately that there were no more than 38 of them -- 38 of them. But I think that there were 35 according to what I remember, so according to what I remember there were between 35 and 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were they all men?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us this place where they were brought to the road, how far is that from the intersection in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Three to 4 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who were the prisoners handed over to physically?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The prisoners were handed over physically to three senior officers, I think, of Dusko Jevic's, and Dusko Jevic was there present when we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you testified recently in Bijeljina precisely in a case trying one of the commanding officers of Dusko Jevic's unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood, he was not a commanding officer. I understood that he was a logistics soldier. Perhaps he was a commanding or senior officer, I don't know. And I did testify in the Bijeljina trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Gavric, Mr. Stojanovic has put one question to you which you didn't answer. Did you take down their names, the names of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did anybody else take down the names of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since these were people in civilian clothing, it was logical for me that I as a soldier should not treat them as military prisoners of war since they were not in uniform. I handed them over to Dusko Jevic, according to an order or agreement with Momir Nikolic, and I understood that as far as I was concerned I was done. There were no bad intentions on my part. Had we had any, we would not have had them brought in or handed them over to that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I have put one follow-up question there. You said they were wearing civilian clothes. Therefore you considered them not to be treated as prisoners of war. Why were they prisoners at all? They were just civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area -- area I was born there; thus nobody lived there. According to the order that we received, everything that we encountered in that area it would be normal that we would liberate the area from those people who were not born there and who did not live there; that is one thing. Secondly, we brought them -- we brought them down there and at any point they could have been potential soldiers. And I'm going to tell you about a problem now. There was a problem of a similar nature because commanding officer committed an error from that area when civilian surrendered themselves and then one of those civilians grabbed a rifle and killed a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there's a saying in English: You can't have your cake and eat it. Which now is the case? You said, I would not consider them to be prisoners of war, and at the same time you say they may have been military people and therefore you would never know. Now, what did you do? Did you consider them to be prisoners of war or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not considered them to be captured soldiers but captured civilians when they surrendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next question: What was the basis for capturing civilians? Had they done anything wrong? Had they -- and you were in a military position. What is the authority of a military over innocent civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We as the army had the assignment in that area since no population was living there. So whatever we encountered, that is number one. Number two, we had among them, which can be confirmed by the witnesses, these children -- we had people among them who had weaponry and threw it away. Then first they put up resistance, this renegade group that did not want to surrender. As far as we were concerned at one point when they bear arms we can call them whatever they want but we would consider them enemies and then on the other hand when they surrendered without weapons then as far as we were concerned they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether they ever had been carrying arms before, that might make them still military men, but you considered them civilians. I'm just putting to you at this moment that it seems that you want to have your cake and eat it. It's either of the two. Well, you're nodding no. I'm just putting to you that that is how we analyse at this moment your testimony without drawing any further conclusions, but that there is some contradiction in it. I have another question. They were not free to move, were they, once they were captured civilians? They were still more or less prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the point of time that they surrendered to our units, they were captured, and I said that as far as I was concerned, civilians were -- they were civilians because they were not in uniform. That is one thing. And that is why I handed them over to the police, because the police is entrusted or in charge of civilians and not the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the police would not detain civilians, would they, if they had not gone anything wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was war. It wasn't peacetime for us to be interfering with anyone. They found themselves in our terrain, in terrain that they were not expected to be found in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were moving in the area. Is there anything wrong with that? I mean were they -- was there any legal prohibition for them to move to the next village or the village after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Since this was an ongoing operation, in that operation all people who were peaceful of their own accord or had simply understood that they were supposed to surrender and did surrender in Potocari, that was one thing. All the others who had decided to start moving towards Tuzla decided to do so in a military column that was there. Therefore, that group also was definitely in that column. It's just that they were late. They were lagging behind the main body of the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was there fire from that group at the Army of Republika Srpska as the legitimate military power?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any danger of anybody getting killed, wounded, hit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. Whenever there is shooting, there is the possibility that somebody would be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you brought these people to the road, you sought instructions from the Bratunac Brigade command as to what to do with these people.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in your estimate that could have been between 1700 and 1800 hours on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That could have been most realistically sometime between 1800 and 1900 hours when everything was finished and when we had reached the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic, told you what to do with those people?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the one who told you that you should hand them over to the police structures?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, and I'm asking this for reasons that are completely understandable to us and due to testimonies from previous witnesses, whether you informed Momir Nikolic about the number of people who had been brought to the road?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know or be able to correctly remember that or those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if you informed him about the fact that you had four children that you wanted to bring to the Bratunac Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he suggest anything to you regarding those children?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, he did not, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to put a direct question to you: Are you sure about your recollection that you drove three boys towards Bratunac and placed one in a bus or did all the boys get in the buses and go towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I remember that when we gave the children something to eat, three children we brought them -- we were going in front of the buses. The buses were going behind us. So all together we arrived at the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We placed three children in the Lada Niva vehicle. Could Mr. Stojanovic please begin his question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- could you please, Mr. Stojanovic, start your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was some sort of paramilitary person who tried to harm one of those boys. Did you ever find out who that person was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I found out that this was a volunteer from the Cacak area who was in the 3rd Battalion, but I don't know his name to this day. I do have official information that in the following week after that, in some three or four days he tried to take an electric engine in the black Gubar [phoen] area. It was booby-trapped, and so in the process of doing this, dismantling this, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your earlier testimony, and I'll come back to this, you spoke in more detail about the dangers and the possibility of vengeance that was present between the warring sides. Why do you think there was a real danger that people might give in to their desire for revenge?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: People are very different, and they have all very different notions, and we could see that on the ground. Second, I took instantly the decision that it's better for those children not to go to the collection centre but to live in more normal circumstances like before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You said that -- that the people of that group had fired at you, isn't it, before they were ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gunfire was opened at our units. I got that report from the field, namely from the commander of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you also said that it was the members of that group, isn't it, that had fired at your units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that group of people who surrendered, there was a certain number who did not want to surrender and did not surrender, and they had a clash between themselves whether to surrender or not. Jusupovic can tell you that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question to you is whether the members of that group where you said you took 36 or 38 prisoners, whether they had fired at your units or your army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around Burnice village where these people surrendered, there was a large number of people, and only this number surrendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether these people had ever used their arms or any arms, you don't know; the ones you captured, that were captured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which of them fired, whether some from among those who surrendered or those who fled and did not surrender. We were not able to come close and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be soldierly and would it be correct from the police point of view to check whether perhaps among those people there were some who had shot at a legitimate armed force?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, those people who surrendered to us, apart from the underaged ones who were separated from the others, were able bodied and fit for military service, but we should have formed a military panel to do that job, but it was not up to us. It was up to military security authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. I asked you about your fear of possible incidents of revenge. Do you know that such incidents happened on the ground, that people took revenge on others?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I cannot see -- I cannot say that I saw something for myself. I did what I did as a precaution, knowing that with 99.9 per cent certainty these children would be sent for an exchange, and I don't know through how many hands they would pass before the eventual exchange. But my idea was to have them filmed so that whoever handles them from that time on, they know they can't do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I need ten or 12 more minutes to go through the remaining documents, and I plan to finish within that time. Perhaps I should say now that a part of my examination would be in private session to protect certain names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber would prefer that you do that before the break, then we'll look at the clock. You have another 12 minutes then, and we'll then adjourn at close to 25 minutes past 1.00. Please proceed. Well, when I said adjourn, I meant take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we pull up in e-court P1698. P1698.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document has one more page in B/C/S, and I should like to see the next one. Thank you. That is it. We can then go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the reason I want to see this is the following: Do you recognise the handwriting of your brigade commander Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can see it's his signature, but to be quite frank, after so many years I had forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we can go back to page 1 in B/C/S. From what I was able to see, this is the same text but typed on a teleprinter, and it's exactly the same as the one in handwriting. My young learned friend asked you about the first and the last part of this document, and I want to remove a certain confusion. In this document addressed to the command of the Drina Corps, we read that one of them, meaning one of the four children, spoke to the commander of the sweeping unit about a large number of Muslim troops committing suicide or killing each other, and then comes the sentence quoted to you by the Prosecutor: "We propose that this testimony be recorded by cameras of your press centre." Let me ask you now: Did any of these children tell you about mass murders among Muslim troops and mass suicides?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand this is a reference to yourself when it says that the children spoke about that to the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I really don't know, but I know that I spoke to that child and that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that one of the commanders of the sweeping units was also commander of the 3rd Battalion, Dragan Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It also could be the commander, Dragan Zekic, or perhaps the commander of the unit to which they surrendered, because they were divided into companies and platoons which have a company ran into them first, had its own commander, another company commander was Zekic, and I was the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the four boys shared this information with anyone else but you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't talk to them anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now could we please move into private session because I will be mentioning names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. What I want to know, quite simple question, is whether the information about what the boys had told about suicides, et cetera, whether it was you who passed that on to your command which then resulted in a proposal to have it all filmed, or that it was not you who passed on that information.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that I did tell Pilipovic about this. I don't know if by Pilipovic passed that on further though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier today you were asked whether you had provided the information that was contained in that report. Your answer then was: "I only provided information that they passed on to the press conference to the effect that the children were aged 8 to 14 and all the rest was up to the assistant commander for morale." So you didn't provide that information, as I do understand from your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My previous answer was that it was the assignment of the assistant for morale to do what I told him to do. My main motive and task was for him to do with the press centre what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We take a break. Before we take the break could I ask you, Ms. Harbour, whether your position has changed in any way as far as the need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will need around ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Then I'll give you ten minutes, but as I said before, the Chamber needs some time for a few procedural matters as well. But you'll have your ten minutes, but then we'll be very precise. We'll take the break. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 12 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness could be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, this morning at temporary transcript pages 32 and 33, you discussed a meeting that you went to at the Bratunac Brigade on the morning of the 12th of July, 1995, and you said that at that meeting General Mladic issued an order to Furtula. Could you please tell me who else aside from you and Furtula and General Mladic were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that there were many officers who were carrying out the combat assignment in Srebrenica. I know a number of people by the way they look. I know Furtula by name because I was in the same unit during peacetime when he was in the Han Pijesak operations unit. He was the commander of a company. That's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, the question is who was at the meeting in addition to yourself, Furtula, and Mr. Mladic. You haven't said a word about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that all the commanders were there, all the officers. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I will name a few and if you know any of them, would you please let me know if any of them present at the meeting. Blagojevic, was he present?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that when I was there the commander was not inside, as far as I can remember, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And by "the commander," you're referring to Blagojevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think so. I am saying my commander who was my immediate superior, Colonel Blagojevic who was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you know if Krstic was there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Krstic was not there that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you know if Pandurevic was there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't think that Pandurevic was there either. I know him personally. I don't think that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: What about Vasic? Was Vasic there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I know of Vasic, the man. I never met him to this very day. It's possible that the man was there. Is that man from the police component? I don't think that he was there, because it was just us corps officers, if I can say that. And in essence they are the ones who took part in the operation. I know the names of the persons, but I couldn't tell you with any degree of certainty whether Andric, Trivic, and others were there. I really don't know. I know about Furtula because I knew him personally and it has remained with me as an impression when the commander or the general ordered him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be an audio problem apparently. No need to speak aloud, Mr. Mladic. It has been fixed. Please proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P1509 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, this is a Zvornik CJB dispatch. It's dated 12 July 1995, and if I could draw your attention to paragraph 2. This states that a meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade command at 0800 hours at which tasks were assigned to all participants. And again I repeat this is from the 12th of July, 1995, so the same day that you had your meeting. Were you present at this meeting at 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The command of the Bratunac Brigade was located at the ceramic tile factory which had a large number of premises. Then the operations room as I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I just need to know whether you were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I wanted to say because I said earlier that the general left the operations at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm finished with this document. Today at transcript pages 43 to 44, you were reviewing a proposal by Milanovic, and you were asked: "And then who is being assigned as the co-ordinator of this assignment if he does have the right to command?" And you responded: "If certain assignments are about to begin, the superior officer must appoint a lower-ranking officer who would be responsible for that in the entire area. Like I was responsible for the police unit and the military unit in the same way, according to the way I'm thinking, the Colonel could have appointed Blagojevic as the commander of that complete action in that section of the sweep." Do you recall that testimony? Now, I'd like to show you a document which is P1696. Around halfway down the second paragraph it states: "During the day the brigade commander visited all units which are blocking the enemy retreat. The 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, units of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment, parts of the MUP and the 5th Engineering Battalion defined their tasks and organised their joint action and communications." Now, this document is dated 16 July 1995, and it's issued by Commander Colonel Blagojevic. Does this document demonstrate what we saw in the Milanovic proposal that Blagojevic was in command of these units?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If he received a written order as we see that he did from Milanovic, that means that realistically speaking, he was responsible for the reason that that was the area that was part of the Bratunac Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And these units include the 65th Protection Regiment. This is a Main Staff unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, you asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have maybe one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At temporary transcript page 56 today --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm happy to leave my redirect examination as we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions in re-examination triggered any need to further ask questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means, Witness, that this concludes your testimony in this court. Before you leave the court, I would like to inform you that the issue on which that is the people, persons, found hanging and with the lower part of their bodies destroyed, it has been verified. The CLSS has done a great job in providing us with the verification very quickly, and it turns out that it has not been accurately transcribed. So therefore the way in which you explained it is now confirmed in the transcript as will be corrected. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there are a few procedural matters which -- with which I would like to deal. For the first one, I'd like to go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a few matters. I'd like to read a -- some decisions, and I'd like to start with the decision with regard to expert witness Thomas Parsons. On the 2nd of April, 2013, the Prosecution filed a notice of disclosure of Thomas Parsons' expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules and a motion to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list, requesting to add a one-and-a-half page statement by Parsons and the Prosecution sought the admission of Parsons' CV, the report titled "Methodology report 2001-2008 DNA process," which was dated the 15th of January, 2008, and the one-and-a-half page statement I just referred to. On the 8th of May, the Chamber granted the Defence an extension to make its submissions pursuant to Rule 94 bis. On the 3rd of June, the Defence filed its notice and objection. The Defence did not object to the addition of the one and a half page statement by Parsons to the Prosecution's exhibit list. Considering this and the length and the nature of the document, the Chamber decides to grant leave to add it to the exhibit list. In its Rule 94 bis notice, the Defence challenged the methodology and reliability of the proffered report. The Defence requested that the Prosecution be ordered to supplement its submission or that the Chamber should denied the report's admission into evidence and that Parsons be barred from presenting expert evidence. The Defence further requested the opportunity to cross-examine the witness. The Defence did not challenge Parsons' expertise. Upon review of his CV, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge which may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the evidence to be presented by the Prosecution on the DNA identification of victims, including those listed in indictment Schedule E. It therefore considers Parsons an expert for the purpose of his anticipated evidence before the Chamber. With regard to the Defence objections, the Chamber considers that the Defence will have a full opportunity to explore the alleged flaws in methodology and reliability of the report when the witness appears to testify. The Chamber hereby decides pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules that Thomas Parsons may be called to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Defence, and the Chamber defers its decision on admission into evidence of the tendered report, the CV, and the one-and-a-half page statement until the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I would then like to read a decision by the Chamber on the admission of the expert reports and the CV of Witness Kathryn Barr. On the 28th of February, 2013, the Prosecution filed a notification of its disclosure of the expert reports of Witness Kathryn Barr seeking the admission of nine reports on hand and typewriting and the witness's curriculum vitae pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. While the Defence filed its Rule 94 bis (B) notice on the 2nd of April, 2013, in which it objected to the witness's qualification as an expert and to the admissibility of the reports, in court on the 26th of June, it submitted that it would no longer be opposing the admission of the proffered evidence and would not require Witness Barr to be called for cross-examination. This can be found at transcript page 13437. In light of no objection from the Defence with regard to the admission of the proffered evidence, the Chamber will first consider the expert status of Witness Barr and then decide on the admission of the nine reports and her CV. Witness Barr's CV demonstrates that she had at least 11 relevant years of experience in forensic document review at the time she drafted the first report in 2003. The witness started working as a forensic document examiner for the forensic laboratory of the Metropolitan Police in 1992, before joining her current employer, Document Evidence Limited in Birmingham in 1999, where she now holds the position of director and works as a forensic document examiner. In addition, during her years of experience, the witness has examined documents and handwriting in over a thousand cases, including cases before the Tribunal. Therefore, the Chamber considers that Witness Barr has, through her experience as a forensic document examiner, developed specialised knowledge in forensic document review which may assist the Chamber in understanding the evidence to be presented by the Prosecution in this case. With regard to the requirements of Rule 89(C) and (D) of the Rules, the Chamber finds the proffered evidence to be relevant to the case and probative for the purposes of admission, as the reports assess the authenticity of relevant military documents such as log-books and vehicle logs through the analysis of handwriting entries of alleged JCE members and typewriting respectively. In light of the foregoing and considering that the Defence accepts the proffered evidence to be admitted without calling Witness Barr to testify in person, the Chamber admits the nine reports with 65 ter numbers 05655 up to and including 05659, 06226, 06227 and 06228, and 25909, as well as her CV bearing 65 ter number 05660 into evidence under Rule 94 bis (C), and requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to the respective documents. Madam Registrar, I don't know whether you can already provide us with a range now. I think we need ten. Madam Registrar will provisionally assign numbers and will communicate them through a memo. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If with the indulgence of all those assisting us, I have one other decision to read. It's even shorter. I therefore seek their co-operation. It is the oral decision on the admission of the associated exhibits in relation to Witness RM176. During the testimony of Witness RM176, the Prosecution tendered 16 documents associated with his two witness statements which were admitted into evidence as Exhibits P640 and P641, both under seal. The Registry filed an internal memorandum on the 17th of November -- December 2012, assigning provisional exhibit numbers to the 16 documents. With regard to the numbers -- the number of associated exhibits, the Chamber notes the Defence's objection of the 27th of November, 2012. While the Prosecution has reduced the number of associated exhibits from originally 26 as tendered in the 92 ter motion of Witness RM176 on the 14th of November, 2012, to 16 now, the Chamber uses this opportunity to again remind the parties of its previous guidance to carefully consider the need for each document they tender and to limit the amount of associate exhibits to the extent possible. As neither of the parties made follow-up submissions with regard to the tendered documents, the Chamber will now decide on their admission using the approach taken in the Tucker oral decision of the 22nd of November, 2012. Consequently, the Chamber admits the following 14 documents into evidence as associated exhibits of Witness RM176's statement: P649, P650, P652, P653, and P654, all under seal; P655, P657, P659, P660, P661, P662, P663, P665, P667, all public with the exception of P665 which is admitted under seal. With regard to the two remaining associated exhibits MFI'd as P648 and P666, the Chamber denies their admission into evidence without prejudice. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I think -- yes Mr. Groome. You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have information regarding RM506 if the Chamber wishes to hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it would be good if it will be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

The ones that the Prosecution is proposing to deal with in a bar table are ones that he's unable to address the substance so the Prosecution would be making submission regarding their relevance separately from the ones that he can speak to their substance and that's the reason for distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he would still testify as to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of all exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of all exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Whether it's then really bar tabling or not remains -- remains a question, but at least we now better understand what the request is about. Then I'd like to thank everyone assisting us in this courtroom and around this courtroom for their indulgence, and we resume -- we adjourn for the day and we'll resume Monday, the 8th of July, at 9.30 in the morning, Madam Registrar, in Courtroom III. We stand adjourned.
